profile.summary: RNA-km is a language model for non-coding RNA sequences, built to predict RNA secondary structure, including pseudoknots, without training on labelled structures. It reads a single RNA sequence and returns a 1024-value representation per nucleotide and attention maps. In the paper, the attention maps are turned into base pairs with a minimum-cost flow algorithm.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-km is a BERT-style transformer encoder with 12 layers, embedding dimension 1024 and 16 attention heads, 152 million parameters in total according to the paper. It uses a relative positional encoding instead of absolute sinusoidal positions. It was pretrained by masked language modelling: 15% of bases are masked, and 80% of the masks are contiguous spans of k bases with k from 3 to 8, so the model has to recover whole k-mers. The paper describes the input as the bases A, C, G, U and N; the released code converts U to T and builds its vocabulary from A, T, C, G and X. For structure prediction the paper fits an L1-regularised logistic regression on the attention maps, using 5 RNAs, to give base-pair probabilities, then builds the structure with the minimum-cost flow algorithm of KnotFold; that step is not in the repository files read.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository offers one pretrained weight file, weight.pth, downloaded from Google Drive and placed in a weight folder. No version number, checksum or second checkpoint is given. The paper describes one model, trained with a batch of 1 million tokens for 600,000 steps; the saved files do not tie weight.pth to that run explicitly. The zero-shot structure results also depend on the logistic regression fitted on 5 PDB RNAs, which the repository files read do not include. A result should name the repository commit and note that the weight file comes from the Google Drive link in the README.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Self-supervised RNA language model (foundation model) for zero-shot RNA secondary structure prediction.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Transformer encoder: 12 layers, width 1024, 16 attention heads (the code sets the head count to the width divided by 64), feed-forward width four times the model width, relative position bias (64 buckets, maximum distance 256), plus a pairwise projection of width 512. The paper describes the same 12 layers, width 1024 and 16 heads.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: One RNA sequence in FASTA format. U is converted to T and any letter other than A, C, G or T becomes N.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: A per-nucleotide representation of size L by 1024, saved as a .npy file; with --attn, the attention weights are saved too.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: 152 million, as the paper states for the model with 12 layers, width 1024 and 16 heads. No count is given for the released weight.pth file, which was not downloaded.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Over 23 million non-coding RNA sequences from RNAcentral version 22.0, used without structure labels. Sequences longer than 512 bases were cut into non-overlapping 512-base fragments, which MMseqs2 clustered at 80% identity into 8.9 million clusters; 10,000 clusters were held out for validation and each cluster was sampled with equal probability.

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: One pretrained weight file (weight.pth) linked from the README. No other checkpoints are described.

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: RNAcentral version 22.0. The paper gives no download date.

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: No fixed maximum length is stated. The model uses relative position biases (64 buckets, maximum distance 256) rather than a fixed-length position table. In training, sequences longer than 512 bases were cut into 512-base fragments.

facts.label: Weights licence
facts.value: Not stated separately. The weight file is hosted on Google Drive and the README's MIT statement refers to the repository; no licence specific to the weights is given.

facts.label: Code licence
facts.value: MIT, per the repository LICENSE (copyright 2024 gongtiansu).

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Code: https://github.com/gongtiansu/RNA-km. Weights: Google Drive, https://drive.google.com/file/d/1DI79-R33R396ZdbNcqbADQMP7Nprb_ze/view?usp=sharing.

strengths.text: Designed for zero-shot structure prediction: base-pair probabilities come from the attention maps through a logistic regression fitted on only 5 RNAs, and the authors report F1 scores of 0.627 on 527 PDB RNAs and 0.456 on TR0, against 0.433 and 0.339 for RNA-FM run the same way (the authors' figures).
Small, readable code base under the MIT licence, with a single script that writes embeddings and attention maps to NumPy files.

limitations.text: The repository only extracts embeddings and attention maps. The minimum-cost flow step that turns attention into a secondary structure is described in the paper but is not in the repository files read.
The script reads only the first record of the FASTA file, taking the sequence from the second line, so multi-line or multi-sequence FASTA files are not handled.
The weights are a single file on Google Drive with no version, checksum or stated licence.
The authors report that RNA-FM beat RNA-km mainly on sequences shorter than 100 bases (94 of 95 such cases), and suggest RNA-km was pretrained mainly on long sequences.

profile.summary: PromoterAI is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts how a variant in a gene promoter changes that gene's expression. It takes a list of variants (chromosome, position, reference and alternative allele, strand) and a reference genome, and adds a score between -1 and 1 to each variant: negative values mean lower expression and positive values mean higher expression. The authors built it to find noncoding promoter variants that may explain rare genetic diseases.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Variant effect prediction; Europe PMC abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PromoterAI is a convolutional network written in TensorFlow and Keras. In the paper, a 20,480-base one-hot sequence is widened to 1,024 channels and passed through 24 MetaFormer blocks, each a depthwise convolution and a feed-forward step with batch normalisation and residual connections, with kernel size 5 and dilations chosen to cover 16,384 bases. The outputs of every fourth block are averaged to predict 970 human and mouse regulatory profiles over the central 4,096 positions. The model was first trained on these profiles around annotated transcription start sites, then fine-tuned on rare GTEx promoter variants with known expression effects; only the output layers, about 3 million parameters, were tuned. A variant's score is the alternative minus the reference prediction, averaged over positions and channels.
sections.source_locator: paper: Materials and methods (Model architecture, Model training, Model fine-tuning, Variant score)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper's score is the average of two models: one trained and fine-tuned on human data only, and one on human and mouse data. The README's scoring command takes a single model folder and describes no averaging step. The Python package is at version 1.0rc6 in the repository read here. In June 2025 the authors said they had released the code and precomputed scores but not the model weights; in September 2025 they said the download link is sent by email after the licence agreement linked from the README is completed. The sources read do not name or version the distributed weights, so a result should name the package version, the repository commit, the model folder or folders used and the input length (20480).
sections.source_locator: paper: Model ensemble, Variant score; README.md: scoring; setup.py; issues 3 and 10

sections.title: Scores and thresholds
sections.body: Scores run from -1 to 1. The README recommends cut-offs at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 in absolute value. Because a promoter variant acts through one gene's strand, each variant row needs a strand; if it is unknown, the README says to score both strands as separate rows and combine the results. Precomputed scores for all human promoter single nucleotide variants are available for academic and non-commercial research after the licence agreement.
sections.source_locator: README.md: introduction and Variant effect prediction

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised deep neural network for promoter variant effect prediction on gene expression.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: 1D convolutional network: input widened from 4 to 1,024 channels, then 24 MetaFormer blocks (depthwise convolution with kernel size 5 and a feed-forward step, each with batch normalisation and a residual connection); the outputs of every fourth block pass through a dense layer and are averaged. Output: 970 profiles over the central 4,096 positions.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A TSV of variants with columns chrom, pos, ref, alt and strand, plus a reference genome FASTA file. Single nucleotide variants and left-normalised indels are accepted.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: One score per variant row, from -1 (under-expression) to 1 (over-expression), written as a new column named score in a copy of the variant file.
facts.source_locator: README.md: introduction and Variant effect prediction

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: About 208 million trainable parameters per model, as the paper states; the fine-tuning step tuned about 3 million of them. The published score uses two such models. The distributed weight files are not named in the sources read.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: 970 regulatory profiles (498 human, 472 mouse): ENCODE histone, accessibility and transcription factor tracks (310 human and 192 mouse experiments after filtering) and FANTOM5 CAGE tracks, in 4,096-base windows around 244,939 GENCODE v39 and 81,540 GENCODE vM25 transcription start sites. Fine-tuned on 57,795 rare promoter variants from GTEx v8 with expression effects from RNA-seq.
facts.source_locator: paper: Training dataset, Model training, Model fine-tuning

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: Python package promoterai 1.0rc6 in the repository read here. The sources read do not name the distributed model checkpoints.

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: No date is given. The data versions named are GENCODE v39 and vM25 for the training windows and GTEx v8 for fine-tuning.
facts.source_locator: paper: Model training; GTEx multi-tissue expression outliers

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: 20,480 bases of input sequence, as in the paper and the README scoring and training commands; predictions cover the central 4,096 positions. Training preprocessing writes 32,768-base windows.

facts.label: Weights licence
facts.value: Licence agreement with Illumina; weights are shared by email after the agreement linked from the README is completed. Commercial use is by purchase from Illumina.

facts.label: Code licence
facts.value: PolyForm Strict License 1.0.0: noncommercial use only, no distribution and no changes or new works based on the software. GitHub lists the repository licence as NOASSERTION.
facts.source_locator: LICENSE; setup.py; GitHub API licence field

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Code: https://github.com/Illumina/PromoterAI and the pip package promoterai. Weights and precomputed scores: by email after completing the licence agreement linked from the README. Commercial licences are handled by Illumina; the README gives a contact.
facts.source_locator: README.md: introduction and Installation; issue 10 collaborator reply

strengths.text: Works from plain variant coordinates and a reference genome, and handles both single nucleotide variants and left-normalised indels.
Gives a signed score, so a user can tell predicted loss of expression from predicted gain, and the README gives thresholds to apply.
The authors report a correlation of 0.63 between PromoterAI scores and effect sizes measured for 686 promoter eQTLs in an assay of fine-mapped variants (the authors' figure).
Training, preprocessing and fine-tuning code is included, along with the benchmark and training annotation files, so the model can be retrained.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Model training and fine-tuning; issue 3 collaborator reply

limitations.text: Not open source: the code is under the PolyForm Strict licence (noncommercial, no distribution, no derivative works), and commercial use of scores and models must be bought from Illumina.
The weights are not downloadable directly. They are sent by email after a licence agreement, and the scoring command cannot run without a model folder.
limitations.source_locator: issue 10 collaborator reply; README.md: Variant effect prediction

limitations.text: Each variant needs a strand. If the strand is unknown the user must score both strands and combine the results themselves.

The authors state that the model is limited by the modest number of gene expression measurements available for training, and may miss tissue-specific effects and variants further from the transcription start site.
